Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Oral bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches systemic circulation in unchanged form. It is determined by three sequential barriers: absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen across the intestinal epithelium, first-pass metabolism in the gut wall (primarily by CYP3A4), and first-pass metabolism in the liver (by CYP enzymes and conjugation). This dataset uses a binary threshold of F ≥ 20% vs F < 20%.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) balances membrane permeability with aqueous solubility. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 140 Å²) facilitates transcellular passive diffusion. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.
Question: Given a drug SMILES string, predict whether it
(A) has oral bioavailability < 20% (B) has oral bioavailability ≥ 20%
Drug SMILES: C[C@]12CCC3=C4CCC(=O)C=C4CC[C@H]3[C@@H]1CC[C@@]2(O)CC#N
Please think step by step and use the relevant tools in your analysis.

Begin by examining the molecular structure; identify the core scaffold, substituents, and any reactive or pharmacologically relevant motifs. Use tools to gather quantitative data about the molecule's properties.

Critically, perform structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis: retrieve similar molecules with known labels and compare them to the query. If the accuracy of the neighborhood is low, focus on the contrastive example (the most similar molecule with the opposite label) and reason about which specific structural differences explain the divergent outcome and whether our task molecule has those structural differences. This comparative reasoning is often more informative than absolute property values alone.

Integrate all lines of evidence — physicochemical properties, functional group analysis, structural alerts, metabolic liabilities, and SAR analogy — into a coherent argument. Use your internal chemistry knowledge as well. Weigh evidence for and against each label explicitly before committing to your prediction.

Then put your final choice, (A) or (B), after "Answer:"

It is determined by three sequential barriers: absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen across the intestinal epithelium, first-pass metabolism in the gut wall (primarily by CYP3A4), and first-pass metabolism in the liver (by CYP enzymes and conjugation). This dataset uses a binary threshold of F ≥ 20% vs F < 20%.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) balances membrane permeability with aqueous solubility. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 140 Å²) facilitates transcellular passive diffusion. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.

It is determined by three sequential barriers: absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen across the intestinal epithelium, first-pass metabolism in the gut wall (primarily by CYP3A4), and first-pass metabolism in the liver (by CYP enzymes and conjugation). This dataset uses a binary threshold of F ≥ 20% vs F < 20%.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) balances membrane permeability with aqueous solubility. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 140 Å²) facilitates transcellular passive diffusion. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Oral bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches systemic circulation in unchanged form. It is determined by three sequential barriers: absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen across the intestinal epithelium, first-pass metabolism in the gut wall (primarily by CYP3A4), and first-pass metabolism in the liver (by CYP enzymes and conjugation). This dataset uses a binary threshold of F ≥ 20% vs F < 20%.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) balances membrane permeability with aqueous solubility. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 140 Å²) facilitates transcellular passive diffusion. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.

Instructions: Answer the following question about drug properties.
Context: Oral bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an orally administered drug that reaches systemic circulation in unchanged form. It is determined by three sequential barriers: absorption from the gastrointestinal lumen across the intestinal epithelium, first-pass metabolism in the gut wall (primarily by CYP3A4), and first-pass metabolism in the liver (by CYP enzymes and conjugation). This dataset uses a binary threshold of F ≥ 20% vs F < 20%.

Molecular features favoring high oral bioavailability: compliance with Lipinski's Rule of Five (MW ≤ 500, logP ≤ 5, HBD ≤ 5, HBA ≤ 10) — these are necessary but not sufficient conditions for oral absorption. Moderate lipophilicity (logP 1-3) balances membrane permeability with aqueous solubility. Low polar surface area (TPSA < 140 Å²) facilitates transcellular passive diffusion. Limited molecular flexibility (rotatable bonds ≤ 10) reduces the entropic penalty for adopting a membrane-permeable conformation. Adequate aqueous solubility ensures dissolution in GI fluids. Metabolic stability — resistance to CYP-mediated oxidation and Phase II conjugation — preserves the parent compound through first-pass metabolism.

Features associated with poor bioavailability: high MW (>500 Da) and excessive hydrogen bonding capacity reduce membrane permeability. Very high lipophilicity (logP > 5) causes poor aqueous solubility despite good permeability. High TPSA (>140 Å²) strongly correlates with poor absorption. Many rotatable bonds (>10) reduce the probability of adopting a compact, membrane-permeable conformation. Susceptibility to efflux by P-glycoprotein (Pgp) at the intestinal epithelium reduces net absorption. Labile metabolic soft spots — unhindered aromatic rings, benzylic positions, N-dealkylation sites — lead to rapid first-pass metabolism. Compounds that are substrates of CYP3A4 (the dominant gut-wall and hepatic CYP) face extensive first-pass extraction.
